General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less.
  • It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

According to recent reports, I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching latest lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

It has been revealed that this is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Recent findings suggest that getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

If you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

According to recent reports, when you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a new branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

Industry observers note that in the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

According to recent reports, as the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

It has been revealed that thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for remarked Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

According to recent reports, not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the substantial chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

According to recent reports, what I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing latest folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

In a recent development, I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

It has been revealed that much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a week of GTA 6's availability, there are two things I can say with complete certainty: first, Red Dead Redemption 2 is the best thing that could have happened to Rockstar, and second, we'll be following Jason, Lucia, and company for a long time.

The developer's magnum opus offers an immersive and expansive world that will take us many years to fully decipher, so I can already imagine how numerous ecosystems, from video games to content creation, will be completely permeated until, perhaps, the release of the seventh installment.

However, far from wanting to theorize about future adventures of the IP, the priority is to appreciate the one we already have in our hands and savor it slowly, since that's what the game itself aims for by offering a story, mechanics, and context that evolve at a much more leisurely pace.

Therefore, in order to play fortune teller and anticipate how long we will be hanging around Leonida, I invite you to read this list of ten reasons you will be playing GTA 6 for more than a decade.

Analyzing the evolution of video games, especially considering their affinity with technology, is an activity that involves intertemporal comparisons, and GTA 6 has established itself as the generational benchmark we look to when we want to see if the industry has moved forward.

Titles like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, BioShock, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, and The Last of Us Part II have stood for years as monoliths of their respective genres and platforms, garnering enduring attention that regularly draws us back to reaffirm their influence.

Thus, considering the technical, graphical, and design marvel that is Rockstar's title, particularly within the context of open worlds, it will be impossible for it to escape associations with future representatives of the genre, who will undoubtedly seek to learn from it.

Although comparisons are generally odious, it's also true that they constitute a timely method to contrast the evolution, or involution, of a medium, so I can already see many scholars of this art revisiting its confines to diagnose its eventual state.

While I acknowledge the omnipresence of the internet and our hyper-connected state has made the task of hunting for secrets virtually impossible, I know I'm not the only one who has deliberately avoided all discussion about the game in order to discover it for myself.

By choosing not to use guides, watch gameplay videos, or even compare opinions, the game's lifespan is instantly extended due to its immeasurable size and content, much of which is hidden behind hundreds of hours of spontaneous and meticulous exploration.

You may finish the campaign and feel satisfied with what you've experienced, but for a game that has taken so long to arrive and generated so much anticipation, I'm sure that a large portion of its player base will continue playing until there's no dialogue, NPC, mission, weapon, or random event left undiscovered.

This largely depends on how much you choose to interact with its online discourse, as you will surely encounter spoilers of all kinds as the days and months go by, yet a whole second life awaits you if you choose to turn a blind eye to other people's experiences and strive to discover everything on your own.

Assuming I'm not the only oddball who's spent countless hours wandering around open-world games listening to their tunes without engaging in any particular activity, GTA 6's deep and outstanding soundtrack will behave like a music player with extra steps.

In fact, a large part of my GTA 5 playtime consisted of countless nights spent hopping into any legitimately acquired vehicle and cruising around the city's interiors and exteriors, and after just an hour of playing this new installment, I already knew the future would be the same.

Whether you enjoy pop, urban music, rap, or listening to the radio as if it were real life (which it is closer to than I'd like to admit), there's a station for every type of listener, helping the game also become an album that will remind you of the era in which it was released.

Never underestimate the power of songs as tools to prolong our connection with a video game because, just like with Secunda in Skyrim or I Really Want To Stay at Your House in Cyberpunk 2077, I'm sure RHYNO will have us going around in circles in Vice City for a very, very long time.

A major surprise I encountered in my first few hours of playing GTA 6 was the influence of immersive sims on its mission design, as there isn't just one way to solve many of the main and side objectives in the campaign.

Obviously, we're not talking about the depth of an Arkane Studios title, though there's enough density and player agency to allow for diverse approaches, ranging from peaceful resolutions if you know who to talk to, to stealthy sieges where no one necessarily has to be killed.

Add to that the game's inherent spontaneity, which throws you into special and unexpected encounters every second, all waiting to grab your attention, and you realize its replayability stems from a design specifically intended to be open and multifaceted.

I hope GTA 6's approach helps the genre emerge from its slumber, but while I invoke every possible deity to make that happen, I'm content to return to Leonida every few years to see what fresh interactions Rockstar prepared without me noticing in my first five playthroughs.

In conjunction with the above, the title places a notable emphasis on role-playing elements, influencing both the story and gameplay according to how the player chooses to interact with their world, allowing Jason and Lucia to be canvases with clear forms yet ultimately emphasized by the player.

Between choosing the type of relationship they develop, making choices that influence the narrative at key plot points, and the constant decision-making involved in adhering to (or not) morality and law, you can have completely different experiences if you shift your mindset enough.

According to recent reports, in this sense, for my first playthrough, I have a more restrained and rigorous Jason and a more antisocial and rebellious Lucia within a loving relationship, always acting in accordance with these personality archetypes. Regardless, for my second playthrough, I strategy to take a completely opposite path.

In a recent development, the result? At the very least, one more run with hundreds of hours and variations that will make me even more amazed by the immeasurable talent of the Rockstar workers, to whom I feel I owe the respect of playing the game at least three times to properly appreciate the countless hours they invested in shaping the product.

The third of my three planned playthroughs, designed to fully exploit the game, will consist of not killing anyone unless the game forces me to, which brings us to the mechanism that has kept hundreds of video games alive online: challenge runs.

It has been revealed that beating the entire game with only fists, without breaking any laws, without using money, with only a knife, using only public transport, in the shortest time feasible, as the worst possible partner... I don't know if the possibilities are truly infinite, but they certainly come close.

Games like Dark Souls and Hollow Knight have demonstrated for years that human creativity knows no bounds, especially when it comes to creating content that borders on masochism, so it's only natural that GTA 6 will be like a second home for all these inventive people.

I don't know if I'll be among them, yet my experience being chronically online assures me with complete certainty that GTA 6 will sustain entire communities based on challenges, rising exponentially if mods are added to the equation.

Heraclitus mentioned it's impossible to step into the same river twice because everything changes, both in the river itself and in the person crossing it, and I believe the mythical Greek philosopher made this aphorism with the belief that we would eventually have the boundless body of water that is GTA 6.

Experiences with open worlds, like the aforementioned Skyrim or, more recently, Elden Ring, tend to be special thanks to the organic nature of their worlds, given you feel like you're in an alternate, digital reality where you're truly part of a larger cosmos.

Leonida, however, takes these sensations to uncharted territory, where it genuinely feels impossible to experience the same thing twice because of how reactive and multifaceted its systems are, like hundreds of thousands of windows that only open if you're in the right place at the right time.

This contextual fertility ensures that there will almost always be a new experience to go through, and as long as the flame of belief that there are unexplored horizons remains alive (something that GTA 5 already demonstrated), there will be parishioners who remain absorbed watching the fire, waiting to hear an unprecedented crackle.

The fear of missing out on a cultural event is fascinating because, contrary to popular belief, it can have a timeless quality; for example, it's the reason I played the first iterations of Red Dead Redemption and The Last of Us, even though it was a decade after their respective releases.

Given GTA 6 is and will be a cultural touchstone of modern entertainment, many will return to its realm years later to satisfy a curiosity they perhaps didn't solve at launch for one reason or another, ranging from waiting for a price drop to the complete optimization of its features.

Beyond the causes, and considering a legacy that is already titanic after just one week of release and will become even more staggering as time goes on, it seems that playing GTA 6 will be like watching The Godfather or reading the Odyssey: an essential ritual for understanding the path its medium will take in the future.

Even if you're not a fan of the series or the genre, the curiosity to understand the reasons behind its multi-million sales and resounding unanimous praise as a masterpiece on Metacritic will be compelling for those who value video games as an art form, since great works always deserve attention, even if it's to criticize them.

Rockstar has found its closest model to follow in GTA 5, the same recipe that allowed them to maintain the product's relevance for over ten years with virtually no significant drop in popularity or impact, whose success hinges on spacing out re-releases, which will rekindle the unresolved desires of a significant portion of the gaming community.

Motivated by the release of the PC version and potential upcoming consoles from Microsoft and Sony, or even by the anticipation of a product with as few bugs and inconsistencies as possible, many people will refrain from jumping on the bandwagon at its peak, instead patiently waiting for the waters to calm down.

The 235 million copies sold of its predecessor didn't happen overnight; they materialized gradually and steadily year after year, and it's quite easy to predict that market behavior this time around will be virtually the same.

Many of them are repeat buyers, of course, but that doesn't invalidate the title's statement: whether it's your first time or your fiftieth, the hardware will give you very appealing reasons to discover or check out how GTA 6 is, even if it's 2036.

However, by far, the biggest reason to be sure you'll be playing GTA 6 for more than ten years lies in its multiplayer mode, a fundamental pillar that sustained GTA 5 throughout its lifespan and which, without a doubt, will repeat that feat with this newly introduced installment.

If we assume Rockstar will be able to create a product that surpasses its predecessor as the base game did, the only sensible conclusion about the next iteration of GTA Online is that it will be a candidate for the most massive, complex, and profitable multiplayer experience of all time.

Phenomena like Fortnite or League of Legends cast doubt on such a claim, but the fact that this is even the scale used to measure GTA 6's multiplayer is indicative enough of what it will mean for the franchise and the market once it's released.

More than the sheer scale of its world, more than sociocultural pressure, and more than even any traditional DLC, what could allow Rockstar to go two generations without releasing a game and still be the most popular developer in the world is the online variant of GTA 6.

Not only because of its name and legacy, which also mean a great deal, but because of the game's inherent quality, which suggests that its size, freedom of action, and overall quality will be remarkable enough to carry the Grand Theft Auto name for as long as it lasts.

Breaking: The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a upcoming in-game currency to pay for them

📅 04 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (427 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Vg247

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era.
  • The two newly introduced features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17.
  • The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis confirmed The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two newly introduced destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two newly introduced features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

In a recent development, created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature rolls out, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a upcoming virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

Recent findings suggest that in order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the newly introduced features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

Spirit Crossing, the latest Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • In a recent development, deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • It has been revealed that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in tech giant, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

In a recent development, deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

It has been revealed that there's nothing forcing you to do any of this in tech giant, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Industry observers note that spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

You can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

Industry observers note that as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

Industry observers note that it's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

Latest Update: GTA 6 Might Have A Kingdom Hearts Easter Egg

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thegamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some Kingdom Hearts fans are convinced that they’ve found a reference to the series in Grand Theft Auto 6, but not everyone is so sure it's intentional.
  • As you no doubt know by now, GTA 6 is absolutely chock-a-block with references to other video games.
  • So far, one such series is Kingdom Hearts, which is a little bit of a shame since it’s my all-time favourite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some Kingdom Hearts fans are convinced that they’ve found a reference to the series in Grand Theft Auto 6, but not everyone is so sure it's intentional.

As you no doubt know by now, GTA 6 is absolutely chock-a-block with references to other video games. We’ve seen Mario, Final Fantasy, the original Vice City, Clair Obscur, a surprisingly sharp The Last of Us jab, and oh so much more. In fact, it’s probably easier to say the games that don’t have some kind of easter egg in GTA 6.

So far, one such series is Kingdom Hearts, which is a little bit of a shame since it’s my all-time favourite. You’d think a Keyblade ripoff would be hiding somewhere in Leonida, but that doesn’t appear to be the case just yet. Even if the series’ signature weapon isn't lurking, some fans are sure there’s a nod in there to one of its iconic symbols.

Sources indicate that as pointed out by Redditor Vogcoycoycut on the Kingdom Hearts subreddit, fans have found what they believe to be a reference to the series within GTA 6. It can be found during one of the game’s story missions, where Jason and Dre’Quan go to a watch store that’s clearly meant to be parodying Rolex.

On the floor of that shop is a crown symbol that’s meant to be riffing on the one that Rolex has. Only, in this case, it’s much closer to the crown featured on Sora’s necklace and serves as one of Kingdom Hearts' main symbols. It’s not one-to-one or anything, but it’s incredibly close, and much more so than a generic crown logo.

According to recent reports, while the riff on Rolex and the symbol being featured in a jewellery store (which makes me think of Sora’s necklace) do make it seem like a nod to Kingdom Hearts, there’s also a chance that it’s just a generic crown symbol that’s close to KH and that fans are seeing what they want to see. The thread is clearly very split on whether it’s intentional or not, and I can't blame them.

You could even really stretch by saying that time is a reference to Young Xehanort. Like I say, you’d REALLY be stretching.

In a recent development, that being mentioned, this is Rockstar that we’re talking about, so we know that no detail is included in GTA 6 without at least some thought behind it. It’s still certainly not definitive, but there’s a chance someone at the studio is a massive fan of Kingdom Hearts and wanted to include at least one nod to the series.

I'll just have to remember to be a little more discerning when chasing down one of GTA 6's cars to make sure I don't absolutely ruin the interior from a surprise storm.

It's not going unnoticed by developers outside of Rockstar, either. Emil Pagliarulo, longtime Bethesda developer – with Elder Scrolls gems like Skyrim and Fallout titles under his belt – stands out, taking to X to share his thoughts on the new Grand Theft Auto. "So many articles/posts by game devs saying GTA 6 is SO great," he starts, referencing all of the perfect scores (as our own GTA 6 review gives, too) out there. "Like, the pinnacle of video games! There you have it folks – GTA 6 is "pure sorcery," as per an RPG sorcerer himself. Comments, of course, see fellow fans of the latest Grand Theft Auto toast to that. "It's like playing a video game using a Time Machine to see what games will be like a decade from now," one reads. "It's truly unparalleled.".

#133222. Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • It has been revealed that microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

It has been revealed that microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

Sources indicate that for Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

Recent findings suggest that however, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Consumers were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

In a recent development, in the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

"I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

In a recent development, "The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find new uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

Recent findings suggest that when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the concern of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

According to recent reports, alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering owners.

Recent findings suggest that "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

Grand Theft Auto 6 producer Rob Nelson has admitted that he was “praying” the game’s major plot twist in Chapter 1 didn’t get spoiled ahead of time.

According to recent reports, leading up to the release of GTA 6, it felt like Rockstar had shown us plenty of what the game was about. We had a general idea of Jason and Lucia’s circumstances in Leonida, detailed reports on the game’s expanded mechanics, and enough footage of the world for some dedicated fans to piece together a mapping project.

In a recent development, and, of course, there were the infamous Cyberleek leaks that showed much more than Rockstar ever wanted us to. Now that the game is actually out, though, it’s painfully clear just how little we knew about GTA 6, which all starts in the game’s opening hour when perhaps its biggest plot point is revealed after years of hiding it away.

I’m sure anyone interested is already well past this point, but we’ll be discussing GTA 6’s main Chapter 1 twist below.

I am, of course, talking about the major reveal that Jason and Lucia have a child together, Tomas, who is taken away from them both after Lucia is arrested early on in the game. It’s as much of a surprise to Jason as it is to the players, as Rockstar somehow managed to keep it out of all the marketing and even didn’t get it ruined by Cyberleek.

Sources indicate that VGC’s Jordan Middler recently had the chance to chat to Grand Theft Auto 6 producer Rob Nelson about that surprise moment. Nelson confirmed that Rockstar was “never” going to reveal that plot point, and that he was “praying it stays under wraps” before the game’s launch, especially with “everything that we’ve gone through”.

Nelson is surely referring to just how many leaks GTA 6 was hit with, which somehow didn't result in such a massive point being spoiled.

It has been revealed that nelson went on to say that the twist is meant to shock the player, especially with how much everyone was speculating on Jason and Lucia’s relationship. Like with many of GTA 6’s elements, it’s also meant to take the game and your actions “in a completely different context”, and give you more to aim for than just money.

It has been revealed that of course, while most players were surprised by Jason and Lucia being parents, it’s fair to say that there was at least some speculation about it. Many thought Ryan Gosling’s The Place Beyond the Pines, which has a similar leading duo with a child, was an inspiration point, but I don’t think anyone was certain Rockstar would follow through on such a big story focus.

Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The massive Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods.
  • You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.
  • Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The massive Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Industry observers note that patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies promptly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

It has been revealed that elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a newly introduced activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

In a recent development, the Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a upcoming item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the fresh season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been a big week for videogames—or rather, videogame. Grand Theft Auto 6 is enjoying what may very well be the single greatest media launch in history, securing over $3.7 billion in launch sales. But as Rockstar enjoys its acclaim, other developers—like Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski—are professing some anxiety about releasing their own games in a post-GTA 6 world.

Recent findings suggest that "GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real. Probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, I mean it. Scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle," Sarzynski said on Bluesky over the weekend, joking that "Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled.".

That news came as a surprise to Cyberpunk 2 lead writer Anna Megill, who replied with a baffled "But wait—".

In a recent development, sarzynski was, of course, just goofing. But I'm sympathetic to any game dev who might be feeling an amount of apprehension about being measured against GTA 6's success, particularly when there's a genre overlap.

In a recent development, in Cyberpunk 2's case, however, CD Projekt is very much in its own lane: Cyberpunk is a different thematic setting, with entirely different systems and design goals. I'd hope that any reasonable person would think comparing the two is like comparing apples and oranges—particularly when the oranges reportedly had a production budget upwards of $1 billion.

In a follow-up post, Sarzynski acknowledged that each project is doing its own thing, while noting that GTA 6's example will benefit other game developers by serving as a source of creative inspiration.

"Seriously though, I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor," he said. "GTA is impressive in a way all great art is: It expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • Sources indicate that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a upcoming motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

Recent findings suggest that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

Sources indicate that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a upcoming motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

It has been revealed that "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

Industry observers note that you know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which presently looks likely to last until at least 2028.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Revision, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.
  • The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.
  • It has been revealed that since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Revision, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

It has been revealed that since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

Recent findings suggest that the Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside newly introduced Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Industry observers note that lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Devil May Cry creator Hideki Kamiya states he's interested in tackling the Castlevania series if Konami would hand him the reins.

In his first YouTube video in over a year (translated by Automaton), Kamiya set the record straight on some questions about his newly introduced studio Clovers. Namely, although he's working on Okami – a series he created while at Capcom – he hasn't returned to the publisher, nor is the studio funded by Capcom or any other investors. He also notes that Capcom may not be the only publisher Clovers works with, saying, "Because we're not getting any external funding and we're completely independent, we want to foster a friendly relationship and work together with many different companies, and take on various things from now on.".

Industry observers note that as for the potential collaborators, he (jokingly) notes, "maybe they hate me, but I love Nintendo, so I think we may be able to do something together." Kamiya directed his best game – The Wonderful 101 – at Nintendo, as well as working as a supervisor on the Bayonetta titles and Astral Chain for the manufacturer before leaving Platinum Games. He also notes he'd be up for working with Sony or Microsoft – with the latter having worked with him on Scalebound before its cancellation.

According to recent reports, kamiya lists a number of franchises he'd love to work on, such as Koei Tecmo's Star Force, Square Enix's King's Knight, and Bandai Namco's Tag Team Match: M.U.S.C.L.E., as well as Konami's GetsuFumaDen. However, as far as Konami is concerned, he specifically highlights Castlevania as one he's interested in. "We'll definitely make Castlevania. If you let us work on it," Kamiya notes in a message to the publisher, saying "we can make something truly insane, so just contact us and we'll be at your service.".

In a recent development, as far as character action games go, it's hard to call anyone but Kamiya the GOAT. And the idea of a Castlevania action game – think Lords of Shadow but a little more Devil May Cry than God of War – has been one on my wishlist for a long time. So frankly now I'm going to be disappointed if this doesn't happen.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse was born out of "a sense of urgency," producer claims, and if we have to wait 10 years for the next game, "the whole thing is meaningless.".

Star Wars Galactic Racer will get local split-screen multiplayer in early 2027 with upcoming 'Free Play' mode, finally letting racers yell at one another in a tangible space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Sources indicate that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an matter for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming patch, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially debuted.
  • The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.
  • Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially debuted. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

In a recent development, marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

In a recent development, indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#133207. Feature: 8 Ways To Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time More Difficult
